extracted.intended_audience: media consumers, journalists, bloggers, and readers interested in media ethics and attribution
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating journalistic and blog practices around attribution, originality, and the roles each plays (especially in opinion/analysis). Includes norms for crediting sources and standards for newsroom independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and linking of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Bloggers routinely credit (and link to) the source of the material on which they're commenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explicit credit and a hyperlink to the original source when using or commenting on others' work. The page asserts bloggers are generally much better than traditional journalists at crediting the work of others and presents crediting/linking as a positive practice and a standard to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbatim lifting / plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lift passages from others nearly verbatim without attribution (the Maureen Dowd incident involved admitting to “inadvertently” lifting a passage from a blog post almost verbatim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using text, paraphrase or quote with clear attribution. Check sources before publishing to avoid inadvertent close copying. Admission of ‘inadvertent’ lifting is presented as an ethical lapse; proper attribution prevents such breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms against attribution in some establishment journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an unwritten code among many establishment journalists that while they credit each other’s work, they feel free to claim as their own whatever they find online without any need for credit or attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that cultural newsroom norms can excuse non-attribution; evaluators should judge practices not only by formal rules but by these informal norms. The item is presented as a criticism of that culture and implies a standard: do not adopt non-attribution norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of roles: bloggers vs mainstream press
rubrics_metrics.description: Bloggers and mainstream press fill different roles; there are areas where bloggers have yet to fill roles established by the mainstream press, but opinion and analysis are areas where bloggers can and do match or replace print journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a blog or journalist, assess the function (breaking reporting, investigative work, opinion/analysis). Do not overgeneralize from one domain — treat opinion/analysis differently from roles that require resources or institutional reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent, reader-supported publishing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent outlets that are free of programmatic ads and not behind paywalls answer to readers rather than advertisers or billionaire owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative standard for news organizations, emphasize editorial independence and transparency about funding. The page frames reader-supported, ad-free, non-paywalled publishing as a virtue and a criterion for trustworthiness and commitment to pursuing the truth.
